guide.title: Unit 9: Globalization: review guide
guide.intro: Since 1900, new technologies, economic policies, and international institutions have tied the world closer together. This unit covers advances in technology and medicine and their limits, environmental debates, economic change and the institutions that manage it, movements for rights and reform, and the globalization of culture, along with resistance to it.

sections.title: Technology, disease, and the environment
body: Technologies such as radio, television, cell phones, and the internet sped communication; the Green Revolution's high-yield seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation raised food production in places such as Mexico and India. Antibiotics and vaccines saved millions, and smallpox was eradicated by 1980.

Yet diseases persisted or emerged: the 1918 influenza pandemic, HIV/AIDS from the 1980s, and COVID-19 from 2020, as well as heart disease and other illnesses linked to longer lives. Growing populations and fossil-fuel use caused deforestation, pollution, and climate change, prompting debates and agreements such as the 2015 Paris Agreement.
points: Technological advances often had limits or unequal effects.
Name both benefits and costs of the Green Revolution.

sections.title: Economic change and international institutions
body: After 1945, institutions such as the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund, and the World Bank were created, and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (later the World Trade Organization, 1995) promoted freer trade. From the 1970s, neoliberal policies (privatization, deregulation, and free trade) spread, for example in Chile, Britain, and the United States. After 1978, Deng Xiaoping opened China to market reforms and foreign investment while the Communist Party kept political control.

Regional groups such as the European Union, ASEAN, and NAFTA expanded trade. Globalization also met resistance, from the Zapatista uprising in Mexico in 1994 to protests at the 1999 WTO meeting in Seattle.
points: Distinguish state-led economies from neoliberal market reforms.
International institutions include governments' organizations and non-governmental organizations (NGOs).

sections.title: Reform movements and global culture
body: The UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) set out rights for all people. Movements for civil rights in the United States, women's rights, and an end to apartheid in South Africa, where Nelson Mandela was elected president in 1994, won major changes; environmental activists such as Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement linked ecology and women's empowerment.

Culture spread in many directions: American brands and films, Indian Bollywood films, South Korean pop music, Jamaican reggae, and global sports such as the World Cup. Some groups resisted, defending local traditions or religious identities against what they saw as cultural homogenization.
points: Continuity and change: rights expanded, but inequality and discrimination persisted.
Cultural globalization flowed from many regions, not only the West.

example.prompt: Explain one limitation of the Green Revolution.
example.solution: It depended on costly fertilizers, pesticides, and irrigation, so wealthier farmers gained most, and heavy chemical and water use damaged soils and water supplies in some regions.

misconceptions: Global connections are much older; their speed and scale grew sharply after 1945 and again with the internet.
HIV/AIDS, COVID-19, and other diseases show disease remains a major challenge.
Culture flows from many regions, such as Bollywood films and K-pop.
NGOs such as Doctors Without Borders also act globally.

passages.title: Source A: An interpretation of technology and disease since 1900
text: “The twentieth century transformed how long people lived and how they communicated. Antibiotics such as penicillin, mass-produced from the 1940s, cured once-deadly infections, and a global vaccination campaign eradicated smallpox by 1980. In the 1960s, the Green Revolution brought high-yield wheat and rice, chemical fertilizers, and irrigation to Mexico, India, and other countries, sharply raising harvests, though farmers who could afford the inputs gained most, and soils and water supplies suffered in places. Disease did not disappear: HIV/AIDS spread worldwide from the 1980s, and COVID-19 shut down much of the world in 2020. Meanwhile radio, television, and later cell phones and the internet carried news and ideas across borders almost instantly.”

passages.title: Source B: An interpretation of economic change since 1945
text: “The postwar order rested on new institutions: the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and a trade agreement that in 1995 became the World Trade Organization. From the 1970s, many governments embraced neoliberal policies, selling state industries, reducing regulation, and lowering trade barriers; Chile under Pinochet, Britain under Thatcher, and the United States under Reagan led the way. After 1978, Deng Xiaoping opened China to foreign investment and market incentives while the Communist Party kept political control, and China became a manufacturing giant. Not everyone welcomed these changes. In 1994 the Zapatistas rose in southern Mexico against free trade, and in 1999 protesters disrupted the WTO meeting in Seattle.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of movements for rights and reform
text: “In 1948 the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which declared that all people are born free and equal in dignity and rights. In the decades that followed, movements used such ideals to press for change. In the United States, the civil rights movement won the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In South Africa, decades of resistance and international pressure ended apartheid, and Nelson Mandela was elected president in 1994. In Kenya, Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement organized women to plant millions of trees, linking environmental protection with women's empowerment. Many movements faced arrests and violence, and discrimination persisted even where laws changed.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of global culture and institutions
text: “Global culture after 1950 flowed in many directions. American soft drinks, fast food, and films spread worldwide, but so did Indian Bollywood films, Jamaican reggae, Japanese anime, and South Korean pop music. Sports such as soccer's World Cup drew audiences of billions. Some communities welcomed these changes; others resisted them, reviving religious practices or local traditions as defenses against what they saw as cultural homogenization. Meanwhile new kinds of institutions addressed problems no single state could solve. Non-governmental organizations such as Doctors Without Borders provided medical aid across borders, and in 2015 almost every country signed the Paris Agreement, pledging to limit the greenhouse gas emissions that drive climate change.”
